q: Explain why England and Spain went to war in 1585. (12 marks)

content.h: Para 1 – Dutch Revolt and Treaty of Nonsuch
pts: Elizabeth had secretly funded Dutch Protestant rebels against Spanish Catholic rule since the 1560s
1584: Dutch leader William of Orange assassinated; Elizabeth could no longer avoid direct involvement
1585: Treaty of Nonsuch – pledged 7,400 troops and £126,000/year; England and Spain officially at war

content.h: Para 2 – Drake's raids and commercial rivalry
pts: Drake raided Spanish ships and colonies throughout 1570s–80s secretly backed by Elizabeth; stole £400,000 during circumnavigation 1577–80
Elizabeth knighted Drake in 1580 – Philip saw this as open endorsement of piracy and an act of war
English merchants were competing with Spain in the New World; commercial and military rivalry were inseparable

content.h: Para 3 – Religious and dynastic rivalry made war inevitable
pts: 1584: Treaty of Joinville – Philip allied with French Catholics to destroy Protestantism; Elizabeth was a direct target
Mary Queen of Scots' execution 1587 removed the Catholic alternative to Elizabeth; Philip now believed invasion was the only option
Drake's 1587 raid on Cadiz delayed the Armada by a year – but war was already inevitable by this point

name: War with Spain

q: Explain why the Spanish Armada was defeated in 1588. (12 marks)

pts: Drake sent fireships into the tightly-anchored Armada at Calais – Spanish captains panicked and scattered, breaking the defensive formation
Battle of Gravelines: English galleons faster and more manoeuvrable; inflicted significant damage on the disordered Spanish fleet
Drake's 1587 raid on Cadiz had already delayed the Armada by a year and destroyed valuable supplies
After Gravelines, wind blew the Armada north around Scotland and Ireland; over half of the 130 ships were destroyed by storms
Spanish captains unfamiliar with northern waters; Philip's rigid orders gave Medina-Sidonia no flexibility to adapt
Medal issued after the defeat read "God blew, and they were scattered" – contemporaries credited weather

content.h: Para 3 – The Spanish plan was unworkable from the start
pts: Duke of Parma's 30,000 troops trapped in Netherlands by Dutch flyboats controlling shallow coastal waters – could never link up with the Armada
Plan required impossible coordination across the sea with no direct communication between Medina-Sidonia and Parma
Even without English tactics or storms, the Armada could never have achieved its objective – defeat was built into the plan

name: Spanish Armada

q: Explain why life changed for ordinary people in the reign of Elizabeth. (12 marks)

pts: Permanent theatres built in London from 1570s; 1 penny for standing room – theatre became accessible to all social classes
Brought drama, comedy and ideas to ordinary Londoners in a genuinely new way
Entertainment diversified beyond traditional bear-baiting and cock-fighting; cultural life in London expanded significantly
1572 Vagabonds Act punished vagabonds; 1576 Act for Relief of the Poor was more constructive – Houses of Correction, organised funding
First time government took organised responsibility for the poor rather than leaving it to the Church
Recognising poverty as a social problem requiring a response, not just a moral failing to be punished

content.h: Para 3 – Education expanded access to learning
pts: 72 new grammar schools during Elizabeth's reign; male literacy rose from 20% to 30%
Some middle-class boys could now access education that had previously been restricted to the wealthy and clergy
However girls were entirely excluded and rural poor had no access – change was real but limited in scope

name: Lives of ordinary people

q: Explain why poverty increased in the reign of Elizabeth. (12 marks)

content.h: Para 1 – Population growth drove up prices and pushed down wages
pts: Population rose from 3 million to 4 million – food prices rose as demand increased; more people competing for the same jobs drove wages down
Little ice age: temperatures dropped; harvests more likely to fail; food shortages more frequent
Real purchasing power of ordinary people's wages fell throughout the reign

content.h: Para 2 – Enclosure deprived the poor of land
pts: Wealthy landowners enclosed common land to farm sheep for the profitable wool trade; poor people lost land they depended on for food
Many became landless and drifted to towns looking for work – swelled urban poor and numbers of vagabonds
Debasement of the currency by Henry VIII had created inflation that continued throughout Elizabeth's reign

content.h: Para 3 – Poor relief was inadequate to address the problem
pts: Traditional poor relief through Catholic monasteries had been removed by Henry VIII's dissolution – replaced by nothing for decades
1572 Vagabonds Act focused on punishment rather than addressing the causes of poverty
1576 Houses of Correction were a step forward but could only help limited numbers; underlying causes were never tackled

name: Increase in poverty

q: Explain why voyages of exploration increased during the reign of Elizabeth. (12 marks)

pts: Drake's circumnavigation (1577–80) brought enormous prestige; Elizabeth knighted him on deck of Golden Hind – exploration became socially desirable
Elizabeth's own patronage gave voyages royal endorsement; explorers became national heroes
The prospect of fame was a powerful incentive in a society where reputation and honour mattered enormously

content.h: Para 2 – Profit from the Slave Trade and raiding
pts: 1562: Hawkins created the Triangular Slave Trade – Elizabeth personally invested; vast profits possible
Drake stole £400,000 of Spanish treasure during his circumnavigation – profit and fame were inseparable motivations
Financial backing from Elizabeth and London merchants was driven by economic calculation

content.h: Para 3 – New technology made long voyages possible
pts: Mercator map (1569): more accurate world geography; astrolabes used stars to navigate more precisely at sea
Improved galleon designs made longer ocean voyages safer and more survivable
These advances meant voyages that had previously been impossible became achievable for Elizabethan sailors

name: Exploration

q: Explain why the colonisation of Virginia failed in the 1580s. (12 marks)

content.h: Para 1 – Loss of The Tiger created immediate crisis
pts: Supply ship The Tiger ran aground on arrival 1585; seawater destroyed most food stores – colonists immediately dependent on Algonquians
1587 expedition: colonists arrived too late to plant crops; supply ships forced to return to England
Armada crisis 1588 prevented supply ships returning until 1590 – by which time the colony had vanished

content.h: Para 2 – Conflict with the Algonquian people destroyed any chance of survival
pts: Relations broke down as colonists tried to take food by force when supplies ran low
Algonquians blamed English for spreading disease ("invisible bullets") – created mutual hostility
Ralph Lane's pre-emptive attack and killing of chief Wingina ended any possibility of cooperation essential to survival

content.h: Para 3 – Poor planning made failure likely from the start
pts: Roanoke Island had a shallow harbour unsuitable for large supply ships – a logistically poor choice
Too many soldiers and merchants; not enough farmers with skills to be self-sufficient
England's first generation of colonisation; inexperience meant fundamental mistakes were almost inevitable

name: Virginia colony
hints: Relations with the native Algonquian people

q: "Elizabeth's greatest challenge when she became queen in 1558 was the threat of foreign invasion." How far do you agree?

pts: At war with France; Calais lost; £227,000 debt made it impossible to fund effective military response
Scotland had Auld Alliance with France and was ruled by Catholic Mary QoS; potential Catholic invasion from north and south simultaneously
If France and Spain had united against Protestant England the consequences could have been catastrophic

content.h: Disagree A – religious division equally serious
pts: Catholics believed Elizabeth was illegitimate – challenged her basic right to rule, not just her security
1/3 of nobles were Catholic; any religious settlement risked alienating powerful domestic allies; Religious turmoil created internal instability
Religious division gave foreign powers a domestic foothold to exploit – the two threats were inseparable

content.h: Disagree B – financial weakness was the root problem
pts: £227,000 debt made every other challenge worse – could not fight wars, fund diplomacy or rebuild the army
Without money no other problem could be solved; Parliament's control of taxation limited Elizabeth's independence
Debt was the foundation of all her other difficulties – Mary Queen of Scots was dangerous partly because England was too weak to respond

name: Challenges in 1558

q: "Elizabeth effectively settled the problem of religion in England in 1559." How far do you agree?

pts: Via Media satisfied most people: Protestants got Protestant services; Catholics could pay 1 shilling fine and practice privately
Act of Uniformity avoided religious civil wars like those in France (1560s) – England remained relatively stable
Archbishop held the line against Puritan pressure in the Vestment Controversy; the Settlement remained broadly intact

content.h: Disagree A – Puritan challenge continued throughout the reign
pts: Vestment Controversy caused damaging public disputes within the Church; Crucifix Controversy showed the Settlement could be altered under pressure
Puritans repeatedly used Parliament and Privy Council connections to push for further Reformation
By the 1580s some Puritans were establishing Presbyterian structures outside the Settlement – a genuinely separatist challenge

content.h: Disagree B – Catholic threat remained unresolved
pts: Pope's excommunication 1570 turned every English Catholic into a potential traitor – the Settlement could not prevent this
Ridolfi, Throckmorton and Babington plots showed Catholic opposition continued throughout the reign
Required Walsingham's entire intelligence network to maintain – not truly settled if it needed this constant enforcement

name: Religious Settlement

q: "The Catholics posed the greatest threat to Elizabeth's Religious Settlement." How far do you agree?

content.h: Agree – Catholics posed the greater external threat
pts: Pope's excommunication 1570 gave Catholic threat an international dimension – all Catholics religiously obliged to remove Elizabeth
Ridolfi, Throckmorton and Babington plots all threatened Elizabeth's life with potential foreign military backing
Spanish Armada 1588 was a direct Catholic military invasion – could not have been mounted by English Catholics alone

content.h: Disagree A – Puritans threatened from within government
pts: Two Privy Councillors (Dudley and Walsingham) were Puritan supporters; Puritans had significant influence in Parliament
Vestment Controversy caused public disputes; Crucifix Controversy showed they could win concessions from the Settlement
Unlike Catholics, Puritans were already inside the power structure – they could not be excluded without weakening Elizabeth's own government

content.h: Disagree B – Catholic threat was limited in practice
pts: Most Catholic nobles paid recusancy fine rather than rebel – threat was more potential than actual throughout
Spain and France were always distracted when Catholic plots needed their support
Walsingham uncovered every Catholic plot before it could succeed – consistently ineffective in practice despite appearing dangerous

name: Threats to Religious Settlement

q: "The Catholic threat to Elizabeth increased mainly because of the threat of invasion." How far do you agree?

content.h: Agree – foreign invasion threat escalated the danger
pts: Pope's excommunication 1570 provided Spain and France with religious justification for invasion – transformed domestic discontent into international threat
Spanish Armada 1588 was the culmination – a direct invasion attempt backed by the most powerful Catholic monarch in Europe
Without possibility of foreign military support, English Catholics alone lacked the numbers to pose a serious armed threat

content.h: Disagree A – Mary Queen of Scots was equally important
pts: Mary's presence in England from 1568 made her the anchor for every Catholic conspiracy for 18 years
Ridolfi, Throckmorton and Babington plots were all possible because Mary Queen of Scots existed as an alternative monarch – not primarily because of invasion plans
Mary's execution 1587 largely ended the Catholic plot threat; confirms she was the central domestic element

content.h: Disagree B – domestic plots were serious in themselves
pts: Bond of Association 1584: Privy Council so worried about domestic plots they pledged to kill Mary if another plot occurred
Babington Plot had Mary's direct written involvement and required Walsingham's full intelligence network to control – a genuine domestic conspiracy
Catholic plots from English Catholics alone required enormous effort to contain – not simply a foreign invasion threat

name: Catholic threat
hints: Relations with Philip II of Spain

q: "The Puritans were never a serious threat to Elizabeth's Religious Settlement." How far do you agree?

pts: No alternative monarch to replace Elizabeth – challenge was to the Settlement's details, not her right to rule
Vestment Controversy ended with Archbishop insisting vestments remain; Elizabeth could resist Puritan pressure when she chose
A small and divided group; even with Privy Council support they could not force fundamental changes to the Settlement

content.h: Disagree A – Puritans had real political influence
pts: Two Privy Councillors were Puritan supporters – influence at the very heart of government; could shape policy from within
Puritan MPs used Parliament repeatedly to push for further Reformation against Elizabeth's explicit wishes
Crucifix Controversy showed they could win real concessions – crucifixes removed from all churches; real change to the Settlement achieved

content.h: Disagree B – Puritan challenge was sustained throughout the reign
pts: Challenged the Settlement not once but repeatedly – Vestment Controversy, Crucifix Controversy, Parliamentary campaigns throughout the entire reign
Forced Elizabeth to defend her Settlement publicly again and again – not a trivial or occasional nuisance
By the 1580s some Puritans were establishing Presbyterian structures outside the Settlement – a genuinely separatist challenge that went beyond protests

name: Puritan threat

q: "Religion was the main reason for the Revolt of the Northern Earls." How far do you agree?

content.h: Agree – religion was central to the revolt
pts: Marched under banner of the Five Wounds of Christ; tore up Protestant prayer books in Durham Cathedral; celebrated Catholic Mass
Stated aim was to restore Catholicism and remove the Protestant Settlement imposed from the south
The north had remained more Catholic than the south; religion gave the revolt its popular support among ordinary people

content.h: Disagree A – political grievances drove the earls personally
pts: Earls resented being marginalised by Elizabeth's Protestant advisers, particularly William Cecil
Traditional families had ruled northern England but had been replaced by Elizabeth's Council of the North – loss of status and power
Revolt was as much about restoring aristocratic influence as restoring Catholicism – the two were inseparable for the earls

content.h: Disagree B – Mary Queen of Scots was the catalyst that made rebellion possible
pts: Mary's arrival and imprisonment in the north gave the revolt its specific political objective – placing her on the throne
Without Mary as an alternative monarch the revolt would have had no clear aim beyond opposing the Settlement
Revolt planned to free Mary and marry her to the Duke of Norfolk – a political coup that used religious language as justification

name: Northern Earls

q: "The plots and revolts against Elizabeth were never a serious threat." How far do you agree?

pts: Revolt of Northern Earls 1569 collapsed when no other Catholic nobles joined; Elizabeth raised 14,000 soldiers; crushed easily
Walsingham's intelligence network uncovered every plot before it could succeed; allowed Babington Plot to run to gather maximum evidence
If the government defeated every threat over 15 years, they were a persistent nuisance rather than a genuine danger to Elizabeth's throne

content.h: Disagree A – plots were serious in intent and potential
pts: Babington Plot had Mary's direct written involvement and potential Spanish backing – if Walsingham had not intercepted communications it might have succeeded
Even the Northern Earls raised a real army and marched on Durham – only their misjudgement about foreign and noble support prevented a serious challenge
Bond of Association 1584 – a formal collective pledge to kill Mary – was not a proportionate response to a trivial danger

content.h: Disagree B – Mary's existence made the threat ongoing and structural
pts: Mary Queen of Scots' existence as an alternative monarch meant Catholic opposition always had a focal point to organise around
Once Mary was executed 1587 the Catholic plot threat largely ended – confirms the threat was real and serious while she was alive
Three plots in 15 years required Walsingham's entire intelligence network to contain – the profile of a sustained and serious threat

name: Plots and Revolts

q: "The plots and revolts against Elizabeth failed mainly because of a lack of foreign support." How far do you agree?

content.h: Agree – lack of foreign support was crucial
pts: Northern Earls revolt 1569: captured Hartlepool waiting for Spanish troops that never arrived; when they did not come, the revolt collapsed
Ridolfi Plot 1571 depended on Philip II sending Spanish troops; he ultimately held back; English conspirators were exposed without military backing
Without foreign military support, English Catholics alone did not have the numbers or resources to overthrow Elizabeth

content.h: Disagree A – Walsingham's intelligence was equally important
pts: Walsingham intercepted Mary's communications and allowed Babington Plot to run until he had irrefutable evidence
Throckmorton Plot was uncovered before Spain could be mobilised – plots failed because they were detected, not only because foreign support was unavailable
Even with foreign backing, Walsingham's network would likely have known in advance and allowed England to prepare a response

content.h: Disagree B – domestic Catholic weakness was also a fundamental problem
pts: Most English Catholic nobles refused to rebel even when plots were active – personal risk too high regardless of foreign backing
Revolt of Northern Earls failed because no other nobles joined – domestic base for Catholic rebellion was too narrow
Plots required both foreign assistance AND successful domestic organisation – they failed on both counts, not just one

name: Plots and Revolts

q: "Mary Queen of Scots was executed mainly because of pressure from Elizabeth's Privy Council." How far do you agree?

content.h: Agree – Privy Council was the decisive factor
pts: Walsingham spent years building the legal case against Mary; allowed Babington Plot to run specifically to obtain written evidence of her guilt
Bond of Association 1584 pledged the Privy Council to kill anyone who conspired to benefit from Elizabeth's death – made execution automatic
When Elizabeth signed the warrant, Privy Council rushed it through without waiting for final royal confirmation – they acted on their own initiative

content.h: Disagree A – Mary's own actions made execution unavoidable
pts: Mary's direct written approval of plans to assassinate Elizabeth gave undeniable evidence; very hard for Elizabeth to refuse to act after this
Linked to three separate plots over 18 years – Ridolfi, Throckmorton, Babington; her continued existence made every conspiracy possible
Walsingham could only get the evidence by allowing the plot to run – but Mary's own decision to write approving assassination provided it

content.h: Disagree B – Elizabeth was more willing than she claimed
pts: Elizabeth had resisted executing Mary after two previous plots – by 1586 she had effectively run out of arguments
Elizabeth signed the death warrant – the signature was her decision, not the Privy Council's, regardless of what happened afterwards
Her theatrical display of horror at the execution may have been politically motivated to distance herself from Catholic backlash rather than genuine surprise

name: Execution of Mary QoS

q: "The decline in Anglo-Spanish relations 1569–85 was mainly due to Elizabeth's actions." How far do you agree?

pts: Secretly funded and armed Dutch rebels against Philip's rule throughout the 1570s; Treaty of Nonsuch 1585 made this open and official
Knighted Drake in 1580 after theft of £400,000 of Spanish treasure – open endorsement of acts Philip regarded as acts of war
Mary Queen of Scots' execution 1587 removed the Catholic alternative to Elizabeth; Philip decided invasion was the only option

content.h: Disagree A – Philip's own actions also caused deterioration
pts: 1584: Treaty of Joinville with French Catholics pledging to destroy Protestantism – Elizabeth was a direct target before Drake's raids escalated
Philip supported the Ridolfi Plot 1571 – actively sought to overthrow Elizabeth long before war was declared
Philip's brutal suppression of The Dutch Revolt drove Protestant refugees to England and made English support for Dutch rebels popular and rational

content.h: Disagree B – religious rivalry was the root cause of deterioration
pts: Spain and England were natural rivals: largest Catholic power vs leading Protestant power; Pope's excommunication 1570 made this official
Commercial rivalry in the New World was structural – not caused by any individual's actions but by competing imperial ambitions
Deterioration was gradual and mutual; both sides made choices that worsened relations throughout the period

name: War with Spain

q: "The Armada was defeated mainly because of the weather rather than English actions." How far do you agree?

pts: Storms off Ireland and Scotland destroyed over half of the 130 ships – far more destruction than English guns caused
Spanish captains unfamiliar with northern waters; Philip's rigid orders gave Medina-Sidonia no flexibility when conditions changed drastically
Medal read "God blew, and they were scattered" – Elizabethan contemporaries themselves credited weather

content.h: Disagree A – English tactics were crucial
pts: Fireships at Calais broke the Spanish crescent formation – without this the Armada might have regrouped successfully
Battle of Gravelines: faster English galleons inflicted significant damage on the disordered Spanish fleet
Drake's 1587 raid on Cadiz delayed the Armada by a year and gave England crucial time to prepare its defences

content.h: Disagree B – the Spanish plan was unworkable from the start
pts: Parma's 30,000 troops trapped in Netherlands by Dutch flyboats – could never get out to link up with the Armada regardless of Poor communication between commanders
Plan required impossible coordination across the sea with no direct communication
Even without English tactics or storms the Armada could not have achieved its objective – defeat was built into the plan itself

q: "There was a significant improvement in access to education in Elizabeth's reign." How far do you agree?

content.h: Agree – grammar school expansion was significant
pts: 72 new grammar schools during Elizabeth's reign – real expansion in formal education provision
Fees based on income allowed some middle-class boys to attend alongside nobility
Male literacy rose from 20% to 30% – a measurable improvement in educational outcomes during the reign

content.h: Disagree A – the poor and rural people remained excluded
pts: Grammar schools charged fees the poor could not afford; rural majority had virtually no access to formal schooling
Education was designed to fit the station you were born into – not to create social mobility
For the majority of Elizabeth's subjects, access to education did not change at all during the reign

content.h: Disagree B – women were completely excluded from improvement
pts: Girls did not attend school at all; Female education – female literacy remained at 10% throughout the entire reign with no improvement whatsoever
Noble women were educated privately but this was available to only a tiny fraction of the female population
To say access "significantly improved" ignores the fact that half the population – all women – saw no change at all

name: Education

q: "Entertainment in Elizabethan England continued to be based on violence." How far do you agree?

pts: Bear-baiting, bull-baiting and cock-fighting were popular across all social classes throughout the reign; Elizabeth herself enjoyed these spectacles
Public executions and the pillory drew large crowds as entertainment; these were not declining in popularity
The aristocracy continued to hunt as a central social activity; violent entertainments showed no signs of dying out

content.h: Disagree A – Theatre was a genuinely new non-violent entertainment
pts: Permanent theatres from 1570s (The Theatre, The Rose) attracted thousands for 1 penny; Shakespeare's plays offered drama and comedy based on language
Theatre shows Elizabethan entertainment was diversifying – not simply continuing old violent traditions
For the first time ordinary Londoners had access to a rich cultural experience that did not involve violence or blood

content.h: Disagree B – court entertainment had always been non-violent
pts: Nobility enjoyed hunting, hawking, real tennis, music, dancing – a rich range of non-violent pastimes at court
Elizabeth's court was renowned for music, poetry and dancing; she herself was an accomplished musician
To say entertainment "continued to be based on violence" ignores the rich non-violent cultural life that existed at every level of society

name: Leisure

q: "Life for ordinary people improved during Elizabeth's reign." How far do you agree?

pts: 72 new grammar schools; male literacy rose 20% to 30%; theatre open to all for 1 penny – real improvements in cultural access
1576 Houses of Correction built; organised poor relief created; first government responsibility for the poor
For some – particularly in London and among artisan classes – cultural life and access to services genuinely improved

content.h: Disagree A – Inflation and poverty increased for most ordinary people
pts: Population rose from 3 to 4 million – food prices rose, wages fell due to Inflation; the Malthusian Crisis made life materially harder
Enclosure deprived rural poor of common land essential to their subsistence throughout the reign
For the rural poor – the majority of the population – life was measurably harder at the end of the reign than at the start

content.h: Disagree B – improvements were narrow in scope and reach
pts: Theatre in London benefited urban Londoners; rural majority had no access to these cultural gains
Educational improvements benefited middle-class boys; girls were entirely excluded; the poor could not afford fees
Poor relief legislation helped limited numbers; the scale of poverty far exceeded what any Elizabethan law could address

name: Ordinary lives

q: "Poverty increased during Elizabeth's reign mainly because of changes in agriculture." How far do you agree?

content.h: Agree – agricultural change was a major cause
pts: Enclosure drove families off common land they had depended on for subsistence – creating a large class of landless labourers
Shift from arable to sheep farming reduced demand for agricultural labour – same land now employed far fewer people
For rural England specifically, Enclosure was probably the most direct driver of increased poverty

content.h: Disagree A – Population rise was equally important
pts: Population rise from 3 to 4 million increased competition for jobs and food; employers could lower wages; prices rose
Population rise affected urban workers with no connection to agricultural land – enclosure alone cannot explain their poverty
Little ice age: harvest failures independent of enclosure made food prices more volatile and poverty more severe

content.h: Disagree B – financial factors were also significant causes
pts: Debasement of the currency by Henry VIII created inflation that persisted throughout Elizabeth's reign
This eroded the real purchasing power of wages for urban workers entirely independent of any agricultural change
Several overlapping causes combined: attributing poverty "mainly" to agriculture is an oversimplification of a complex problem

name: Causes of poverty

q: "Attitudes towards the poor barely changed during Elizabeth's reign." How far do you agree?

pts: Distinction between "deserving" and "undeserving" poor persisted completely unchanged throughout the reign
1572 Vagabonds Act: whipping and ear-burning – harsh punitive approach reflecting belief that poverty was a moral failing
Exaggerated rumours about criminal Vagabonds persisted throughout the reign; popular attitudes never fundamentally changed

content.h: Disagree A – legislation showed changing official thinking
pts: 1576 Act for the Relief of the Poor: Houses of Correction built; local officials required to find work for poor; wealthy required to fund relief
A shift from pure punishment toward practical support – recognising poverty as a social problem requiring organised response
The 1576 Act was a genuine departure from the purely punitive approach of the 1572 Vagabonds Act

content.h: Disagree B – attitudes varied by group and changed gradually
pts: The deserving/undeserving distinction itself showed some compassion – old and disabled recognised as genuinely needing help
Elizabethan poor law developed across several pieces of legislation (1563, 1572, 1576) – shows evolving thinking, not static attitudes
To say attitudes "barely changed" is too absolute; the 1576 Act's constructive approach was a genuine change from earlier Tudor thinking

name: Attitudes to poverty
hints: Act for the Relief of the Poor (1576)

q: "Voyages of exploration increased in Elizabeth's reign mainly because of the opportunity for fame." How far do you agree?

content.h: Agree – fame was a genuine motivating factor
pts: Drake's circumnavigation brought enormous national prestige; Elizabeth knighted him on deck of the Golden Hind – exploration became socially desirable
Elizabeth's patronage gave exploration royal endorsement; accounts of Drake's exploits were widely read and celebrated
Fame and national glory were powerful incentives in a society where reputation and honour mattered enormously

content.h: Disagree A – profit was more important than fame
pts: Elizabeth personally invested in Hawkins' Triangular Slave Trade expeditions – economic calculation drove royal backing
Drake stole £400,000 of Spanish treasure during his circumnavigation – profit and fame were inseparable motivations
Without the prospect of profit, London merchants would not have funded the voyages that made exploration possible

content.h: Disagree B – new technology made voyages newly possible
pts: Mercator map 1569, astrolabes and improved galleons meant voyages that had been impossible before became achievable
Without these technological advances, desire for fame or profit could not have produced results
Technology enabled the age of exploration – desire for fame was the motivation but the Mercator map and new ship designs were the enabler

name: Exploration

q: "The failure of the Virginia colony in the 1580s was mainly due to Native American resistance." How far do you agree?

content.h: Agree – conflict with Native Americans was significant
pts: Relations with Algonquian chief Wingina broke down as colonists tried to take food by force when supplies ran low
Algonquians blamed English for spreading disease ("invisible bullets"); created mutual hostility and suspicion
Ralph Lane's pre-emptive attack killing Wingina ended any possibility of the cooperation essential to survival

content.h: Disagree A – poor planning was more important than Native American resistance
pts: Loss of The Tiger on arrival in 1585 left colony immediately vulnerable – before any serious conflict with Native Americans had occurred
Too many soldiers and merchants; not enough farmers with practical skills to be self-sufficient – Poor planning from the outset
Roanoke Island chosen with a shallow harbour unsuitable for large supply ships – a fundamental logistical error

content.h: Disagree B – bad timing and external events were decisive
pts: 1587 expedition: colonists arrived too late in the year to plant crops; supply ships forced to return to England immediately
Armada crisis 1588 prevented any supply ships returning until 1590 – by which time the colony had vanished
The 1587 colony's failure owed almost nothing to Native American resistance – it was caused by supply failure and bad timing

name: Virginia colony

q: Explain why the Weimar Republic was unpopular in the period 1919–23. (12 marks)

content.h: Para 1 – Treaty of Versailles and Dolchstoss
pts: June 1919: forced to accept £6.6bn reparations, loss of 13% of land, army limited to 100,000, 100% war guilt – all blamed on Weimar politicians
Called "November Criminals" – accused of stabbing the undefeated army in the back by signing the armistice 11 November 1918
Treaty gave extremist parties a permanent grievance to exploit – the founding political wound of the Weimar period

content.h: Para 2 – Political violence from left and right
pts: January 1919: Spartacist revolt – Luxemburg led 100,000 workers; Ebert used right-wing Freikorps to crush it
1920: Kapp Putsch – Freikorps seized Berlin; army refused to act; only workers' general strike saved democracy
376 politicians assassinated in these early years; government threatened from both left and right simultaneously
France invaded the Ruhr 1923; government printed money to pay striking workers – bread rose from 1 mark (1919) to 200 billion marks (November 1923)
Middle classes lost savings permanently; working class could not keep up with prices
Made abstract political resentment into lived economic catastrophe; directly fuelled extremism and the Munich Putsch

name: Weimar early problems

q: Explain why the Weimar Republic became more stable in the years 1924–29. (12 marks)

pts: November 1923: Rentenmark introduced – halted hyperinflation; tied to land value not printed money
1924: Dawes Plan – reparations cut to £50m/year; $200m US loans secured to stabilise economy
1929: Young Plan – reparations cut to £2bn extended to 1988; extremist support fell from 40% (1924) to 28% (1928)
1925: Locarno Pact – Germany accepted Versailles borders; France left the Ruhr; diplomatic success restored national confidence
1926: Germany joined the League of Nations – accepted back into the international community as a legitimate state
These achievements undermined the nationalist argument that Weimar had failed Germany internationally

content.h: Para 3 – Hindenburg's election gave conservatives confidence in the Republic
pts: 1925: war-hero Hindenburg elected President – conservatives who had opposed the Republic now more willing to support it
Traditional conservatives who might have backed the Nazis instead supported Hindenburg and Weimar's stability
This removed a key political constituency from the extremists and made the Weimar system appear more legitimate

name: Weimar recovery

q: Explain why life improved for some Germans in the years 1924–29. (12 marks)

pts: Rentenmark ended hyperinflation; Dawes Plan secured $200m US loans; wages rose 25%; unemployment fell
100,000 new houses built; war veterans received pensions; real improvement in material conditions for those in work
For those with jobs the mid-1920s saw genuine improvement after years of hyperinflation and political violence
Women gained equal voting rights to men in the Weimar constitution; began working in traditionally male jobs
Wore modern fashions (flappers); more independent social activities; Women's rights were more advanced than in most of Europe
Represented a real transformation from pre-war Imperial Germany for many women, especially in cities
Weimar Germany became the centre of modern European Culture; Bauhaus school developed modern affordable design
Fritz Lang's Metropolis (1927) and Otto Dix's art showed German culture at the cutting edge of European modernity
Berlin became one of the most culturally exciting cities in the world – however prosperity was built entirely on US loans

name: Weimar Golden Years
Hitler gains control of DAP
q: Explain why Hitler was able to gain control over the German Workers' Party (DAP) in the years 1919-21. (12 marks)

content.h: Para 1 – Personal appeal transformed the party
pts: Hitler joined the DAP in 1919 as an army spy – it had just 23 members led by Anton Drexler; he was made head of propaganda and co-wrote the 25 Point Programme (1920) with Drexler outlining nationalist, anti-democratic and anti-Semitic views

His powerful and charismatic speeches grew membership from 23 (1919) to 3,000 (1920) to 20,000 (1923) – people joined because of Hitler personally, not the party; he was simply too important to the party's growth for Drexler to resist
By 1921 Hitler challenged Drexler for leadership and won; he surrounded himself with loyal supporters; his personal following made him impossible to remove

Hitler rebranded the party as NSDAP (1920); introduced the swastika logo and the party newspaper Völkischer Beobachter; the 25 Point Programme gave the party a clear nationalist, anti-Semitic and anti-Weimar identity that had not existed under Drexler

The messaging was deliberately simple and emotionally powerful – promising to tear up Versailles, destroy Communism and restore German greatness; it appealed directly to the grievances of ordinary Germans humiliated by the Treaty
Propaganda gave the party a coherent identity that attracted a mass following; Hitler's communications skills transformed the party's public profile entirely

Hitler set up the SA (Stormtroopers) under Röhm with 800 members by 1922 – gave the party a paramilitary force that could intimidate opponents and protect meetings; the SA projected strength and discipline
At the Bamberg Conference 1926 Hitler cemented the party as an extremist far-right party and silenced left-wing Nazi leaders – organisational control matched his rhetorical dominance
Hitler transformed a tiny fringe group of 23 into an organised mass movement of 20,000 in just four years through both personal charisma and systematic party-building

q: Explain why Hitler attempted the Munich Putsch in 1923. (12 marks)

content.h: Para 1 – Economic crisis created the opportunity
pts: Hyperinflation had made Weimar deeply unpopular by 1923; government appeared helpless; bread cost billions of marks
France's Ruhr invasion added national humiliation to economic chaos; the moment seemed perfect for radical action
Nazi Party had grown to 20,000 members – Hitler felt he had sufficient support to act

content.h: Para 2 – Mussolini's example and Ludendorff's support gave Hitler confidence
pts: October 1922: Mussolini's March on Rome – fascists marched on Italian capital; King made Mussolini Prime Minister; Hitler hoped to replicate this
War-hero General Ludendorff's support gave the coup military credibility and public appeal
Hitler believed Ludendorff's involvement would persuade the army to follow rather than fire on their former commander
Nazi Party had grown to 20,000 members
SA led by Ernst Rohm were becoming a powerful force in Munich
Hitler, incorrectly, believed that the Bavarian leader Gustav Von Kahr would support his revolution.

name: Munich Putsch

q: Explain why the Nazis were unable to gain large amounts of support in the years 1924–28. (12 marks)

content.h: Para 1 – Aftermath of Munich Putsch weakened the party
pts: Nazi Party banned after Putsch; Hitler served 9 months; on release had to rebuild party from scratch
Without the party organisation, momentum from the 1923 crisis was lost; the most promising window of opportunity had closed
Hitler switched to electoral strategy but building a national electoral machine from scratch took years

content.h: Para 2 – Stresemann's economic recovery removed the conditions for extremism
pts: Rentenmark (1923), Dawes Plan (1924) and Locarno Pact (1925) gradually stabilised Germany
As economy improved and international standing recovered, extremist parties lost their appeal
Extremist support fell from 40% (1924) to 28% (1928) – Stresemann's success directly undermined the Nazis' core message

content.h: Para 3 – Hindenburg's election gave conservatives confidence in Weimar
pts: 1925: election of war-hero Hindenburg as President gave conservatives who had opposed the Republic reason to support it
Traditional conservatives who might have backed the Nazis instead supported Hindenburg and Weimar's stability
In 1928 Nazis won only 12 Reichstag seats – in a period of relative prosperity there was simply no market for extreme solutions

name: Nazi Lean Years

q: Explain why support for the Nazi Party increased in the years 1929–32. (12 marks)

content.h: Para 1 – Wall Street Crash and unemployment
pts: October 1929: Wall Street Crash; US banks recalled loans; businesses went bankrupt; unemployment reached 6 million by 1933
Brüning nicknamed "hunger chancellor" – Weimar appeared completely helpless; people were desperate for radical change
Nazi Reichstag seats grew from 12 (1928) to 230 (July 1932) – almost entirely because of the economic crisis

content.h: Para 2 – Fear of communism and business funding
pts: Wealthy businesspeople feared economic chaos would bring Communist revolution; bankrolled the Nazis – funded propaganda, rallies and SA expansion
Nazi electoral success was partly built on class Fear of communism; the Nazis became the shield against the KPD for those with property to lose
SA projected disciplined image of organised strength that contrasted with the chaos of Weimar politics

content.h: Para 3 – Hitler's personal appeal and targeted propaganda
pts: Hitler's charismatic speeches tailored to different audiences: "Arbeit und Brot" for workers; price guarantees for farmers; national restoration for middle class
Goebbels ran sophisticated propaganda using radio, posters and rallies – Nazis far more effective at political communication than other parties
Promised to tear up the Treaty of Versailles – exploited 10 years of built-up resentment at national humiliation

name: Nazi growth in support

q: Explain why Hitler became Chancellor in January 1933. (12 marks)

content.h: Para 1 – Nazi electoral success created pressure on Hindenburg
pts: July 1932: Nazis won 230 seats – largest party in Reichstag; democratic logic pointed to Hitler being given power
13 million votes for Hitler in April 1932 presidential election; Hindenburg had run out of arguments for ignoring the largest party indefinitely
However Nazi support was actually falling by November 1932 (196 seats) – Hitler's appointment was not inevitable from electoral success alone

content.h: Para 2 – Failure of alternatives left Hindenburg with no options
pts: Von Papen (May 1932) could not control Reichstag; forced to resign after six months
Von Schleicher (November 1932) asked Hindenburg for permission to create a military dictatorship – Hindenburg refused
By January 1933 Hindenburg had genuinely run out of viable alternatives; Hitler was the only politician who could command a Reichstag majority

content.h: Para 3 – Von Papen's fatal miscalculation handed Hitler the chancellorship
pts: Von Papen convinced Hindenburg that Hitler could be "controlled" with himself as Vice-Chancellor and a majority of non-Nazi ministers
"Mouse in my pocket" – Von Papen believed he could use Hitler's popularity while retaining real power
30 January 1933: Hitler appointed Chancellor; Von Papen's catastrophic miscalculation became clear within 18 months

name: Becoming Chancellor

q: Explain why Hitler was able to create a dictatorship in the years 1933–34. (12 marks)

content.h: Para 1 – Reichstag Fire provided the legal pretext
pts: 27 February 1933: Reichstag burned; Dutch Communist blamed; 4,000 Communists arrested that night; Communists banned from their 81 seats
This gave Nazis the crucial 2/3 majority required to change the Constitution legally
March 1933: Enabling Act – gave Hitler power to pass any law without the Reichstag; democracy legally abolished

content.h: Para 2 – Banning all opposition destroyed any legal resistance
pts: All other parties banned July 1933; trade unions banned; local government abolished – Germany became a one-party state within months
Police state established: Gestapo, SS and Dachau (1933) created overwhelming atmosphere of terror
No legitimate political opposition left through which resistance could be organised

content.h: Para 3 – Night of the Long Knives and Hindenburg's death completed the process
pts: 30 June 1934: Röhm and ~400 others murdered; army's loyalty secured – they agreed to swear personal oath to Hitler in return
2 August 1934: Hindenburg died; Hitler combined Chancellor and President into title of "Führer"
Process took just 18 months – from Chancellor to complete dictator – using legal mechanisms throughout

name: Creating dictatorship

q: Explain why the Nazis were able to control the German people in the years 1933–39. (12 marks)

pts: Gestapo created such fear that citizens informed on neighbours, parents and friends – self-policing made resistance almost impossible to organise
SS: 300,000 members; above the law; ran Dachau (1933); could arrest, interrogate or execute without trial
Punishment for dissent so severe that most people chose compliance even if they privately disagreed
Goebbels: 45 minutes of Nazi content before every film; radios blocked foreign broadcasts; Nuremberg rallies with 200,000 people
Censorship removed all alternative viewpoints: newspapers closed; books burned; art and culture "Nazified"
Combination of positive Propaganda and negative censorship created an information environment where opposition was invisible

content.h: Para 3 – Genuine support from economic success
pts: Unemployment fell from 6 million (1933) to 500,000 (1939) – many Germans had genuine material reason to support the regime
Hitler Youth (compulsory 1936) and League of German Maidens indoctrinated an entire generation
Fear, propaganda and economic improvement combined – most Germans either genuinely supported or passively accepted Nazi rule

name: Nazi control
Goebbels and propaganda
q: Explain why Joseph Goebbels was able to influence the attitudes of the German people in the years 1933-39. (12 marks)

content.h: Para 1 – Control of media and propaganda
pts: Goebbels was named head of the Reich Ministry of Public Enlightenment and Propaganda; controlled all public information; all films preceded by 45 minutes of Nazi propaganda; Nazi leaders broadcast on radio with loudspeakers set up on street corners across Germany

Nuremberg rallies organised each year with 200,000 people and 20,000 flags – carefully staged to project an image of total Nazi power and popular support; Leni Riefenstahl's Triumph of the Will (1934) glorified Nazi power for cinema audiences across the world

Propaganda was about spreading ideas the Nazis wanted Germans to believe – it was total, relentless and professionally executed; Goebbels understood that repetition and spectacle were more powerful than argument
Critical newspapers closed; radios specifically designed to block foreign broadcasts; books by Jewish and Communist authors publicly burned in mass events across German cities

All art, music and films had to be approved – heroes were always Aryan, villains Jewish or Communist; without any alternative viewpoint, propaganda was far more effective as people could not compare Nazi claims to other perspectives

The combination of total propaganda and total censorship created an information environment where opposition was invisible; self-censorship became widespread as people knew the consequences of dissent

content.h: Para 3 – Culture and sport normalised Nazi rule
pts: Berlin Olympics 1936 used as a global propaganda showcase – huge stadiums covered in eagles and swastikas; Germany won the most medals; showed the world a strong, modern, confident Germany; Jesse Owens' four gold medals was an embarrassment but Goebbels managed the domestic narrative

KdF (Strength through Joy) provided leisure activities – concerts, theatre trips, holidays and cruises previously only available to the wealthy; 35 million KdF members by 1936; culture and leisure normalised Nazi rule and created genuine popular enthusiasm that pure political propaganda could not achieve alone

By embedding Nazi ideology into everyday cultural life – sport, art, music, leisure – Goebbels made support for the regime feel natural rather than coerced; this was arguably his most effective and lasting achievement

q: Explain why some groups opposed the Nazis in the years 1933–39. (12 marks)

content.h: Para 1 – Church opposition challenged Nazi control of religion
pts: 1933: Concordat signed with Pope Pius XI neutralised Catholic opposition – but many individual priests still spoke out
Confessing Church set up 1934 by Pastor Niemöller to oppose the Reich Church; 6,000 priests joined; ~800 sent to concentration camps
Church had its own institutional identity and moral authority that was difficult for the Nazis to completely suppress

content.h: Para 2 – Youth groups resisted Nazi conformity
pts: Swing Youth: teenagers from wealthy families listened to banned American jazz – cultural resistance to Nazi conformity
Edelweiss Pirates: attacked Hitler Youth members, went on hikes, told anti-Nazi jokes – more active resistance
Only 25% of young people attended Nazi Youth groups voluntarily before made compulsory 1936 – broader resistance than is sometimes assumed

content.h: Para 3 – Workers and political opponents continued quiet resistance
pts: Social Democrats continued underground newspapers; workers sometimes damaged machinery or stayed off sick
Some army officers opposed Hitler's leadership – culminating in the July 1944 assassination attempt
Police state was too efficient and terror too severe for organised resistance to grow – opposition remained fragmented throughout

name: Opposition to the Nazis

q: Explain why women's lives changed under the Nazis in the years 1933–39. (12 marks)

content.h: Para 1 – Ideology of the 3 Ks reversed Weimar gains
pts: Nazis believed in Kinder, Kirche, Küche – hated the "new women" of 1920s Weimar who had entered male jobs
Professional women removed: banned from teaching, medicine, law and civil service; girls banned from grammar schools from 1937
The 3 Ks represented a dramatic reversal for professional women who had gained independence during the Weimar period

content.h: Para 2 – Financial incentives changed women's decisions
pts: Marriage loan of 1,000 marks if wife gave up work; a quarter cancelled per child – powerful economic incentive
Mother's Cross medal: bronze for 4 children, silver for 6, gold for 8 – motherhood elevated as patriotic service
These policies shaped the decisions of many women who might otherwise have continued working

content.h: Para 3 – Economic necessity eventually reversed Nazi gender ideology
pts: By late 1930s rearmament required more workers; 1937 marriage loans cancelled; women directed back into factories
The regime's own economic needs forced it to reverse its gender ideology – women returned to work in large numbers
Shows the limits of ideology when it conflicted with the demands of military rearmament and economic production

name: Women under the Nazis

q: Explain why the Nazis tried to control young people in the years 1933–39. (12 marks)

content.h: Para 1 – Future loyalty required indoctrination from childhood
pts: Hitler wanted a "1,000 Year Reich" – children of Germany would carry his ideas long after he died
Boys trained in Hitler Youth for military service – over 1 million trained to shoot guns; physically and mentally prepared for war
Girls in League of German Maidens trained to be wives and mothers – producing the next generation of soldiers and workers

content.h: Para 2 – Control of Schools ensured Nazi ideas shaped a generation
pts: All teachers required to join the Nazi Teachers' League; curriculum rewritten; "Heil Hitler" at start of every lesson
Anti-Semitism and racial hygiene taught as science; history emphasised German greatness and Nazi ideology
Control of Schools meant an entire generation understood Germany's history and its enemies through a Nazi lens

content.h: Para 3 – Hitler Youth organisations extended Nazi control beyond school
pts: 1933: all youth groups banned except Nazi ones; Hitler Youth and League of German Maidens became compulsory in 1936
Only 25% attended voluntarily before 1936 – many needed to be compelled; genuine enthusiasm was more limited than it appeared
Compulsory membership ensured Nazi indoctrination continued outside school hours and away from parental influence

name: Young people

q: Explain why unemployment decreased in Germany in the years 1933–39. (12 marks)

content.h: Para 1 – Rearmament was the most important factor
pts: Conscription introduced 1935; army grew from 100,000 to 1.3 million by 1939 – hundreds of thousands of direct military jobs
Weapons factories, aircraft plants, shipyards – Rearmament created millions of industrial jobs across Germany
Secretly at first then openly from 1935; Hitler broke the Versailles military restrictions deliberately and publicly

content.h: Para 2 – RAD and public works provided employment
pts: RAD (National Labour Service): set up 1933; compulsory 6 months from 1935; built roads, planted trees; pay very low
Autobahn programme employed thousands in construction; also a propaganda showcase for German engineering achievement
These programmes genuinely reduced unemployment numbers, though conditions and pay were poor

content.h: Para 3 – Statistics were manipulated to exaggerate the scale of recovery
pts: Official fall from 6 million to 500,000 overstated the reality – women, Jews and concentration camp prisoners excluded from the count
KdF promised Volkswagen cars to workers who saved; money collected but cars never delivered
Real reduction in unemployment was genuine but the RAD statistics exaggerated how complete and beneficial the recovery was

name: Decrease in unemployment
Workers' lives
q: Explain why the lives of workers changed in the years 1933-39. (12 marks)

content.h: Para 1 – Removal of rights and exploitation
pts: Trade unions banned May 1933 and replaced by the DAF (German Labour Front) which served businesses not workers; workers could no longer strike or negotiate wages; DAF controlled all workplace relations entirely
The SdA (Beauty of Labour) improved facilities – better lighting, canteens, washing facilities – but workers had to carry out improvements themselves in their own time for no extra pay

The Volkswagen scheme promised workers a car if they saved 5 marks a week – 336,000 workers saved; not a single car was delivered; money was diverted to fund rearmament; workers were systematically deceived

content.h: Para 2 – KdF leisure and apparent benefits
pts: KdF (Strength through Joy) organised leisure activities – concerts, theatre trips, sports facilities and cruises to Norway and the Mediterranean previously only available to the wealthy; 35 million KdF members by 1936

Designed to make workers feel Nazism was improving their lives and to keep them occupied outside work hours; for many workers the benefits were real and meaningful even if political freedoms had been entirely stripped away
The combination of apparent benefits and removal of rights created compliance; workers gained leisure but lost the ability to improve their pay or conditions through collective action

content.h: Para 3 – War economy: longer hours not higher wages
pts: From 1936 rearmament increasingly dominated the German economy; the Four Year Plan (1936) prepared Germany for war – workers in armaments factories worked longer hours as production demands escalated relentlessly

Conscription from 1935 meant young men left the workforce; women were directed back into factories from 1937 as rearmament created acute labour shortages; wages did not keep pace with rising cost of living

By the late 1930s real wages had fallen; working hours had increased; the war economy revealed the fundamental contradiction between Nazi promises to workers and the realities of an economy being prepared for total war

q: Explain why the lives of Jewish people in Germany changed in the years 1933–39. (12 marks)

content.h: Para 1 – Early discrimination from 1933 showed anti-Semitism was central to Nazism
pts: April 1933: national boycott of Jewish shops; SA stood outside to intimidate customers; Jews banned from professions
This immediate discrimination showed anti-Semitism was central to Nazism from the very start – not a later development
Propaganda reinforced anti-Semitic stereotypes; books by Jewish authors publicly burned

content.h: Para 2 – Nuremberg Laws 1935 removed legal status
pts: Stripped Jews of German citizenship; banned from marrying non-Jews; classified as a separate race
Gave legal backing to discrimination that had previously been informal; Jews were now a legally defined inferior category
Clear escalation from social and economic discrimination to full legal persecution – a fundamental change

content.h: Para 3 – Kristallnacht 1938 marked the shift to organised violence
pts: 9–10 November 1938: thousands of synagogues and Jewish businesses destroyed; over 100 killed; 30,000 arrested and sent to camps
Jews fined 1 billion marks for "the damage" – showed complete powerlessness of Jews in Nazi Germany by 1938
Marked shift from legal persecution to organised state violence; a major step on the road to the Holocaust

name: Jewish persecution
